consolidation.llm_summary: Consolidation is the FIRST element of the Price Delivery Cycle and 'the beginning of everything.' It occurs when market price creates a range between two defined points (a trading range). Consolidation indicates the LACK of a trend. Its importance: (1) It creates Liquidity to Move Market — breakout traders place pending orders on both sides of the range (above resistance, below support). The more consolidation, the more liquidity accumulates, and the stronger the subsequent move. (2) After consolidation, we always expect a BIG MOVE. The size of consolidation correlates with the size of the next expansion move. Retail traders see the upper level as resistance and lower level as support, placing breakout orders that become the fuel (liquidity) for Smart Money's expansion move.
key_rules: Consolidation = price moving in a defined range (trading range) between two points
Consolidation indicates LACK of trend
Consolidation creates Liquidity on BOTH sides — breakout traders place pending orders
More consolidation → more liquidity → stronger subsequent move
After consolidation → always expect a BIG MOVE
It's the beginning of everything — Price Delivery Cycle starts with consolidation
Retail sees upper = resistance, lower = support → their orders become SM's fuel

expansion.llm_summary: Expansion is a sign of Trend Continuation — equivalent to Break of Structure (BOS). It occurs when price moves quickly (in form of speed/displacement) after consolidation. Its importance: (1) Expansion indicates the footprints of Smart Money entering the market. Where Smart Money enters, market expands with quick speed and displacement. (2) Entry zones are found NEAR THE START of expansion — bullish/bearish order blocks, liquidity voids/price imbalances, and supply/demand zones are all located at the point where expansion begins. This is because Smart Money entered at that point, so entering near it gives the best entry. Expansion mostly follows consolidation.
key_rules: Expansion = sign of trend continuation = Break of Structure (BOS)
Expansion occurs when price moves quickly (speed/displacement) after consolidation
Expansion = indication of footprints of Smart Money entering market
Entry zones are NEAR THE START of expansion
Entry zone types: Order Blocks, Liquidity Voids/Price Imbalance, Supply/Demand Zones, FVGs
Where expansion starts = where Smart Money entered = best entry point
Expansion mostly follows consolidation

retracement.llm_summary: Retracement (also called Pullback or Correction) occurs mostly AFTER expansion. When market expands (moves quickly in one direction), it creates price imbalances — zones where only buy-side or sell-side candles exist without the other side. These imbalances are called Liquidity Voids or Fair Value Gaps (FVGs). Retracement happens when market makes small pullbacks to balance these imbalances — to fill the liquidity voids and FVGs. The market corrects the price imbalance through retracement, then continues in its original trend direction. Importance: Where there is a Fair Value Gap or Liquidity Void, if market returns in the form of retracement, we know it's correcting the price imbalance — not reversing. After filling/correcting, market continues its original expansion direction.
key_rules: Retracement = Pullbacks = Correction within the price range
Retracement mostly occurs AFTER expansion
Purpose: to balance price imbalances (Liquidity Voids / Fair Value Gaps)
Expansion creates zones with only buy or sell candles = price imbalance
Market retraces to fill/correct these imbalances, then continues original direction
FVG/Liquidity Void identification: zone with 3 buy candles and no sell candles (or vice versa)
Retracement ≠ Reversal — it's correction, not trend change

reversal.llm_summary: Reversal is a sign of Change of Character (CHoCH) — when price trend direction changes from bullish to bearish or vice versa. Importance: (1) Reversal gives a WARNING to trend-following traders that the trend is about to change, so they should plan their buy/sell models accordingly. (2) Reversal mostly happens where market grabs a Large Liquidity Pool — this connects to the Sweep-Based CHoCH Model from V10. When market hunts down and sweeps a large liquidity pool, reversal follows. The reversal point is where market changes its trend direction after sweeping liquidity (e.g., at a double top where engineered liquidity gets swept).
key_rules: Reversal = sign of Change of Character (CHoCH) = trend direction change
Reversal gives a WARNING to trend traders to adjust buy/sell models
Reversal mostly happens where market grabs a Large Liquidity Pool
Connects to V10 Sweep-Based CHoCH Model
Reversal point = where market changes direction after sweeping liquidity
Double top / engineered liquidity sweep → reversal point

price_cycle_rules.llm_summary: The 4 elements (Consolidation, Expansion, Retracement, Reversal) combine into the Price Delivery Cycle with specific rules about which phases can follow which. The basic cycle: Consolidation → Expansion → Retracement → Reversal → Consolidation (and repeat). However, phases are interchangeable with their NEAREST neighbors: Consolidation ↔ Expansion (bidirectional), Expansion ↔ Retracement (bidirectional), Retracement ↔ Reversal (bidirectional), Reversal ↔ Consolidation (bidirectional). CRITICAL RULES: (1) Consolidation can NEVER go directly to Retracement. (2) Expansion can NEVER go directly to Reversal. These are the two forbidden transitions — the diagonal states cannot directly interchange. Only ~2% of the time might market violate these rules (abnormalities). Market ALWAYS follows this cycle. Demonstrated with real market case studies showing: Expansion → Consolidation → Expansion, and Consolidation → Expansion → Retracement → Expansion sequences.
key_rules: 4 elements: Consolidation (Range), Expansion (BOS), Retracement (Pullback), Reversal (CHoCH)
Basic cycle: Consolidation → Expansion → Retracement → Reversal → Consolidation
Phases are interchangeable with NEAREST neighbors only (bidirectional arrows)
FORBIDDEN: Consolidation → Retracement (NEVER directly)
FORBIDDEN: Expansion → Reversal (NEVER directly)
Only ~2% chance of market violating these cycle rules (abnormalities)
Market ALWAYS follows this cycle — price CANNOT move without this cycle
Consolidation ↔ Expansion: most common transition
Expansion ↔ Retracement: expansion creates imbalance, retracement corrects it
Retracement ↔ Reversal: after pullback, either continuation or reversal
Reversal ↔ Consolidation: after trend change, market consolidates
